name: Mantra
editorial_article:
Mantra is the seminal 1995 studio album by New York City hardcore punk band Shelter, marking their transition onto the Roadrunner Records roster. A definitive work of the "Krishnacore" subgenre, the album serves as a vehicle for frontman Ray Cappo’s deep commitment to Hare Krishna religious philosophy and critical social commentary. Musically, the record maintains the high-energy, aggressive foundation of hardcore punk while refining the melodic sensibilities that the band had been developing.

Lyrically, the album is famously intellectual for the hardcore scene, even including a printed manifesto titled "Supersoul" in the original physical release, written by Cappo. Tracks like "Message of the Bhagavat" open the album with a reading from the Bhagavad Gita, signaling the band's intention to use their platform to propagate spiritual messages rather than simply engaging in traditional punk dissent. Though some retrospective critics have labeled it a "tame" rock record compared to the rawest corners of hardcore, at the time of its release, Mantra was widely recognized for its polished, articulate delivery of transcendental thought set against a solid 4/4 beat, cementing Shelter’s role as polarizing but principled spokesmen for their specific corner of the New York scene. The album remains a cornerstone for fans of melodic hardcore who appreciate lyrics that challenge conventional Western secular values.
editorial_pitch: A pivotal 1995 hardcore punk album that blended melodic aggression with the spiritual philosophy of the Hare Krishna movement, establishing a definitive sound for the Krishnacore subgenre.
